notes.meaning: Solomon warns worshippers to watch how they behave when entering God's house. True worship means drawing near to hear and obey God, not just going through external rituals. A foolish person brings sacrifices without repentance, mistakenly thinking physical gifts will please God even while living in wickedness. People should come before God with quiet reverence and a willing heart to obey.

Worshippers are told not to rush into speech or make careless prayers before God. Since God sits in heavenly majesty and humans are frail creatures of the earth, our words should be humble, thoughtful, and few. Long speeches and mindless repetition do not impress the Lord. Sincere prayer requires a calm, collected heart rather than hasty talking.

Just as a day overloaded with business and worry leads to restless, confused dreams at night, so speaking too much exposes the voice of a fool. Multiplying words without thinking shows a lack of self-control and an irreverent attitude toward God. Empty babbling in worship only produces confusion and sin. Wise believers keep their speech simple and focused.

A vow is a solemn promise made to the Lord. Anyone who makes such a promise must fulfill it without delay, because God has no delight in foolish, unfaithful people. Postponing payment shows that a person is reluctant to honor their word to God. What has been promised to the Lord must be paid faithfully and promptly.

differ.view: Some Baptists note that voluntary religious vows belong to the Old Testament and are better avoided under the new covenant because they tend to trap the conscience.

notes.meaning: Choosing not to make a voluntary vow is not a sin, because God does not command anyone to make one. However, making a vow and then failing to keep it brings the guilt of breaking faith and lying to God. It is much better and safer to make no special promise at all than to make one carelessly and fail to perform it. Integrity before God requires keeping every commitment we make.

Careless promises can drag a person into sin and bring God's punishment upon their life. The speaker warns against going to the priest, the messenger of God, to claim that a broken vow was just a harmless mistake. Making light excuses for breaking a promise stirs up God's anger and can bring ruin on the work of one's hands. We must be honest and take responsibility for what we say.

Putting faith in many dreams or multiplying endless, empty words only leads to futility and disappointment. True devotion does not consist in chasing mystical imaginations or speaking excessive religious phrases. The real antidote to all this vanity is to fear God with holy awe and respect. A reverent heart keeps us from being led astray by empty religious talk.

People should not be surprised or lose faith when they see the poor being crushed and justice twisted in government provinces. Human governments often have layers of selfish officials who watch one another to protect their own corrupt power. Above all earthly rulers, however, stands the Most High God, who watches every act of injustice and will bring wicked leaders to judgment. God's ultimate authority comforts those who see unfairness in the world.

The produce of the ground is necessary to sustain every human being, rich or poor. Even the most powerful king depends on the crops harvested by ordinary farmers in the fields. Riches cannot replace basic food, and all earthly power relies on the soil God provides. This shows that all people share the same basic human needs.

Anyone who loves money will never feel they have enough of it, and those who crave great wealth are never satisfied with their income. Earthly wealth cannot satisfy the deeper longings of the human heart, because it was never made to feed the soul. Greed only creates a thirst that grows larger the more it is fed. Seeking contentment in money always ends in disappointment.

When a person's property and goods increase, the number of dependents, servants, and guests who consume those goods multiplies as well. The owner cannot eat or use everything himself, so his extra wealth mostly goes to support more people. His only personal benefit is the fleeting sight of watching his possessions come and go. Possessions bring added burdens rather than extra joy.

A working laborer enjoys sweet, refreshing sleep at night, whether his supper was modest or plentiful, because his honest labor leaves him tired and free from heavy cares. On the other hand, the wealthy person is kept awake by an overstuffed stomach and anxious worry about protecting his riches. Having more possessions often brings more stress than comfort. True rest is a blessing that money cannot buy.

Solomon points out a painful tragedy seen in human life: wealth that is hoarded by its owner only to end up hurting him. Clinging greedily to money can make a person proud, turn their heart away from God, and draw the envy of enemies or robbers. What a person gathered for personal safety becomes the very tool of their misery. Hoarding wealth often ruins the soul that clings to it.

A fortune hoarded through years of labor can vanish in a moment through a bad investment or unexpected disaster. The man who dreamed of passing a large estate to his child suddenly finds his hands completely empty. When his son is born, there is nothing left to give him as an inheritance. Earthly wealth is fragile and can disappear without warning.

Every human being enters the world naked from their mother's womb, and leaves the world in the exact same condition. No matter how much money or property a person gathers through a lifetime of work, they cannot carry a single coin through death. Physical wealth stays behind on earth while the soul stands before God. Life must not be wasted on things that cannot survive the grave.

It is a sorrowful reality that every person departs life just as empty-handed as the day they arrived. Laboring solely to pile up earthly wealth is like trying to catch the wind, because nothing can be kept at death. All the anxiety and sweat spent on temporary treasures end up producing zero lasting profit. We should invest our lives in what endures forever.

A greedy person lives out his days in dark misery, depriving himself of simple comforts and eating with anxiety to save money. When sickness strikes, he responds with bitterness, anger, and dread because illness threatens to take away the wealth he worshipped. Instead of turning to God in repentance, he resents everyone around him and fears the grave. Living for money poisons both health and happiness.

Solomon concludes that it is good and fitting for a person to enjoy food, drink, and the fruits of honest work. God gives us the brief days of our life, and taking pleasure in ordinary daily labor is our proper earthly portion. Work should not be treated as a miserable grind, but received as a place of joyful service. Contentment turns simple daily life into a blessing.

When God grants someone wealth along with the power to enjoy it with a peaceful, thankful heart, that ability is a special divine gift. Wealth alone cannot bring happiness unless God provides the grace to use it well and rejoice in one's labor. Having possessions is an earthly favor, but being able to enjoy them with contentment is a greater blessing from God. We should thank God for both our provision and our joy.

A person who receives God's gift of gladness does not spend his life brooding over life's brevity or sorrowful troubles. God keeps his heart engaged with present joy, balancing out the hardships of labor with genuine peace and gratitude. Instead of fretting over things he cannot control, he walks calmly through his days. A cheerful spirit softens the burdens of this fallen world.
